content: The nitrogen group, also known as Group 15 of the periodic table (previously referred to as Group V or Group VA), is collectively called the pnictogens. This group is characterized by the fact that all its elements possess five electrons in their outermost electron shell. Specifically, there are two electrons in the s subshell and three unpaired electrons in the p subshell. Consequently, these elements are three electrons short of completing their outermost electron shell in their non-ionized state. The most significant element in this group is nitrogen (N), which exists in its diatomic form (N₂) and constitutes the primary component of Earth's atmosphere. Other members of this group include phosphorus (P), arsenic (As), antimony (Sb), bismuth (Bi), and the unconfirmed element ununpentium (Uup). Binary compounds formed by elements in this group are collectively referred to as pnictides. The term pnictogen is derived from the Greek word πνίγειν (pnigein), meaning to choke or to stifle, a property associated with nitrogen. Additionally, the name serves as a mnemonic for the two most common members of the group, phosphorus (P) and nitrogen (N). Historically, the group was also referred to as pentels, derived from the Latin word penta, meaning five, reflecting the earlier naming convention of Group VB. The elements in this group are notable for their chemical stability in compounds, which arises from their ability to form double and triple covalent bonds. This property, however, also contributes to their potential toxicity, particularly in the cases of phosphorus, arsenic, and antimony. When these substances interact with various chemicals in the body, they generate strong free radicals that are not easily metabolized by the liver, leading to their accumulation. Paradoxically, the strong bonding characteristic of these elements reduces the toxicity of nitrogen and bismuth when they are part of molecular structures. This is because these elements form highly stable bonds with other atoms, resulting in molecules that are difficult to break apart and are therefore chemically inert. For instance, diatomic nitrogen (N₂) is used to create an inert atmosphere in situations where noble gases like xenon would be prohibitively expensive. The nitrogen group consists of two non-metals (nitrogen and phosphorus), two metalloids (arsenic and antimony), and one metal (bismuth). All the elements in this group are solid at room temperature, except for nitrogen, which exists as a gas under standard conditions.
